1. Introduction


You're probably here to figure out some unclear aspects of AMP mode. For quick navigation, check the table of contents above.

This mode is designed for those who love this game for its gameplay qualities, for what it offers as a pure RPG. There are no additional cutscenes, new dialogue branches, extra quests, or new endings. Ancient Mega Pack is built exclusively around build-crafting, chaos, and pure gameplay tied to the combat system and inventory management.

This isn't even Baldur's Gate 3 in its usual form — it's a brand new way to play the game. Think of it as free DLC that completely changes how you approach character creation and how you spend your time in the game. And I fully realize that this mode's concept may not click with everyone, so don't sweat it if AMP isn't your thing. It doesn't always mean my work was bad — it just wasn't made for your type of thinking. But I hope you're in my camp.




2. How the Mod Works


Ancient Mega Pack, as you can guess from the name, operates across multiple directions, and like any major game mode, it changes far more than just equipment. Let's break it down:


• Item Randomization. My mode is often called "random loot," which is obviously a half-truth, but that's how it started. You head to a spot where you'd expect to find a specific artifact — but you find something completely different, though still appropriate for your current progression. The main draw of AMP — you never know where the current run will take you, or what characters you'll end up building. This opens up such massive replayability potential that many players have already sunk thousands of hours into this mode and are still itching to start a new run.
• Massive Collection of New Artifacts. This is exactly what I spent two years working on solo — the bulk of the work on this mode. No randomization is going to be worthwhile if we're only talking about the original pool of 300 items. What I had to do was a titanic but absolutely essential effort. I expanded the pool to 2500+ artifacts, and that's exactly what keeps you wondering about what you haven't seen yet, haven't tried yet. The items range wildly: from meme-tier stuff that makes you want to smash your monitor, to perfectly boring pieces that complement your combat strategy flawlessly. Boots, helmets, amulets, rings, morningstars, cloaks, armour, shields, gloves, and much more — not a single equipment slot was left unsaturated.
• The Arcanizer. A full economy of acquiring, exchanging, and arcanizing gear — Planar Coins, Void Capsules, and Runic Shards. It's covered in the "Arcanizer System" chapter.
• Quest and Boss Rewards. Completing quests and slaying major enemies gives you selection windows with themed rewards. More details in the "Quest and Boss Rewards" chapter.
• A Living Difficulty. Every fight scales to your party's level, so the mode stays sharp from the start to the endgame. On top of that sit optional escalation systems such as boss progression, the Pyre and the secret ULTRA mode, ready to dial up as far as your nerve allows. All of it is described in the chapters that follow.




3. The Arcanizer System


The Arcanizer is the central system for acquiring and upgrading equipment in AMP. Instead of endless farming — finite resources and targeted loot. The system consists of three interconnected subsystems: Planar Coins, Void Capsules, and Runic Shards. All three interact with each other, forming a closed resource loop.

Planar Coins

Planar Coins are the currency for activating Void Capsules. The type of coin determines the rarity of the item you'll get from a capsule. There are four types:


• Fey Coin — the most common. Yields Uncommon items. Obtained from Act 1 bosses and story progression.
• Shadowfell Coin — Rare items. Obtained from Act 2 bosses and some Act 3 bosses.
• Astral Coin — Very Rare items. Obtained from the toughest bosses.
• Celestial Coin — Legendary items. The most valuable coin, only dropped by the most powerful bosses.

Coins can be combined: five coins of the same type yield one coin of the next rarity up. Just combine five identical coins in your inventory. This works up to Astral Coins — you can't craft Celestial Coins, those are only obtained directly.

Void Capsules

Void Capsules are portable random artifact generators. They're your primary tool for targeted item acquisition in AMP. Each capsule has a limited number of charges, and the count depends on your game mode — Casual capsules carry the most, Hard ones a little more than Normal but with a far tighter reroll window. When charges run out, the capsule disappears.

How to use a capsule:


• Open the capsule like a container and place a Planar Coin inside.
• A random artifact from that capsule's pool will appear in your inventory. The artifact's rarity is determined by the coin type.
• The capsule loses a charge. Rerolling costs a little more.

Capsules come in two families:

Slot Capsules generate an item for a specific equipment slot. 12 types total: helmets, cloaks, robes, armour, shields, gloves, boots, amulets, rings, one-handed weapons, two-handed weapons, and a generic capsule (any slot).

Themed Capsules generate items from synergy pools — the item can be for any slot, but always matches a specific theme. 10 types total:


• Swamp — acid, poison, webs, hag
• Aquatic — lightning, cold, aquamancy
• Shadowfell — necrotic, shadow, death
• Arcane — wizards, arcana, intelligence, abjuration
• Celestial — radiant, paladins, sunlight, deities
• Nature — druids, healing, summons, rangers
• Destructive — warlocks, force, gravity, blood, thunder
• War — fighters, rogues, martial combat
• Psionic — wisdom, psychic, monks, illithids, gish
• Primal — sorcerers, barbarians, fire, critical hits, bards

Capsules can be found in Interplanar Chests, received as quest rewards, purchased from merchants on your first visit, and bought at the Trials of Tav Shop.

Reroll

When you get an item from a capsule, you don't have to keep it. The item temporarily receives a "Reroll Window" status lasting several turns (the window is generous on Casual and Normal, and noticeably shorter on Hard). While the status is active, you can place the item back into any Void Capsule — it'll be replaced with a new random item from that capsule's pool at the same rarity. Each reroll costs a little extra charge.

Here's the key: you can keep rolling items indefinitely as long as you have capsules with charges and the Reroll Window status is still on the item. One coin — potentially dozens of items to choose from. If you need more time to think, switch to turn-based mode — the status timer will pause until you end your turn.

Salvaging Artifacts

Unwanted equipment can be recycled by placing it into a capsule. If the item qualifies (equippable, valuable enough, valid slot), it'll be destroyed and you'll have a chance to receive Runic Shards. The more expensive the item, the higher the chance — legendary artifacts guarantee shards, while cheap ones rarely yield any. On a fail, the item is still destroyed and the capsule loses a charge.

If you've been unlucky with salvaging for a while, Normal mode has a pity system: after several consecutive failures, AMP guarantees shards.

Converting Shards to Coins

Unwanted Runic Shards can also be placed into a capsule for a chance to receive a Planar Coin in return. That chance depends on the shard's rarity: common shards convert easily, while the rarest convert only occasionally. The coin type matches the shard's rarity: common shards yield Fey Coins, rare ones yield Astral and Celestial. On a fail, the shard is destroyed. This closes the resource loop: shards → coins → capsules → items → salvage → shards.

Runic Shards

Runic Shards are consumable items for permanently arcanizing equipment. AMP features over 100 different shards, each with a unique effect. Shards can be found in the world, obtained through capsule salvaging, purchased from merchants, and bought at the Trials of Tav Shop.

How to arcanize an item:


• Equip the item you want to upgrade.
• Use the shard (right-click → Arcanize). The shard automatically determines the target slot: a glove shard arcanizes your gloves, a weapon shard arcanizes the weapon in your main hand.
• If the required slot is empty, the shard won't be consumed — you can try again.
• On success, the shard is destroyed and the item gains a permanent effect.

Shards come in two types based on stacking. Stackable shards can be applied multiple times to the same item — for example, the Steel Shard (+1 AC) can be applied twice for +2. Non-Stackable shards only work once — a repeat application will be rejected and the shard is preserved.

Shards also split by target slot: weapon shards arcanize the weapon in your main hand, while equipment shards arcanize armour, rings, gloves, helmets, boots, cloaks, and amulets. Some shard families are interchangeable: for instance, elemental weapon shards (fire, cold, lightning, etc.) replace each other, and boot trail shards (fire, ice, acid) do too, so you can only have one from each family on any given item.

Here are some examples to give you a sense of the variety:


• Elemental weapon shards — add a die of a chosen element (fire, cold, lightning, acid, poison, necrotic, radiant, thunder, force, psychic). Interchangeable — you can re-forge your weapon's element to match your build.
• Empowerment Shard — makes a weapon magical with a bonus to attack and damage. Essential for the early game.
• Conduit Shard — the weapon starts using your spellcasting ability for attacks. Every gish and cleric's dream.
• Fatebending Shard — immunity to critical hits. One of the strongest defensive arcanizations in the game.
• Steel Shard — +1 AC, stackable. Simple but universal.
• Weave Shard — a bonus to spell save DC. Stackable. Valuable for any caster.
• Predation Shard — lowers your critical hit threshold. Stackable. Dangerous and effective.
• Trail shards for boots — leave surfaces every turn (fire, ice, acid, water, grease, poison). Interchangeable.
• Elemental specialization shards — for helmets. Boost a specific element (fire, cold, lightning, thunder).
• Ability score shards for amulets — stackable bonuses to each of the six ability scores.

Special mention goes to the Reclamation Shard — a unique shard that extracts all runic shards from all equipped gear, returning them to your inventory. All arcanizations are removed in the process. This lets you fully redistribute your arcanizations when switching builds without losing your invested resources.




4. Quest and Boss Rewards


As you progress, you'll receive rewards for completed quests and kills on major enemies. This all happens through a selection window — you see a list of items and pick what fits your build.


• Five types of quest rewards. Rewards are divided into poor, normal, rich, legendary, and mixed. These types generally correspond to one of four rarities, but don't always offer just one, sometimes exceeding their tier. I'm not going to tell you which decisions to make to get specific rewards — that's part of the adventure.


• Major Act rewards. Beyond regular rewards, there are special major rewards tied to completing Acts. These offer a choice of not just one, but 6-10 rewards from a wide selection.


• Avatar rewards. If you started the game as one of the story heroes rather than Tav, unique avatar rewards await you. They're concentrated in Act 3, though not exclusively, and offer the most powerful random items.


• Boss rewards. Over twenty major bosses across all three Acts have their own themed rewards tied to their lore and combat style. After killing a boss, you'll see a selection window with items thematically matched to that specific enemy: a necromancer offers dark magic, a devil offers infernal relics, and a hag offers deceptively devious artifacts. The rewards are random, but always pulled from that boss's themed pool. This applies to every iconic enemy — from Ethel and Dror Ragzlin in Act 1 to Raphael, Orin, and Gortash in Act 3.


• Chance at rare resources. Any reward — quest or boss — has a small chance to include a Void Capsule, Planar Coin, or Runic Shard among the choices.

Avarice

If the default loot pace feels stingy to you, there's an opt-in switch called Avarice that loosens the purse strings across the whole game. Flip it on from the Training Ring settings or during the opening setup. It's off by default and works in any game mode.

With Avarice on, boss reward windows grow richer: more options to choose from, and an extra tier of quality woven into the pool. Merchants also come stocked with bundles of bonus loot containers, scaled to the Act you're in, ready to be bought and cracked open. Think of it as a generosity dial: nothing in the core balance changes, you simply get more to pick through. If you like the tight, earned economy that AMP is built around, leave it off. If you just want to swim in loot, turn it on and don't look back.




5. Game Modes


At the start of every run, AMP asks you to choose one of three game modes. This isn't just a difficulty setting — each mode defines an entire ruleset affecting economy, resource access, and enemy behavior. The choice is permanent, though you can reassign it through the Training Ring if you change your mind.


• Casual — a relaxed run for those who just want random loot and a good time. Enemies are barely buffed, every escalation system is switched off, and artifacts practically rain on you. Merchants endlessly refresh their magical stock, Interplanar Chests are plentiful and already unlocked, all adamantine moulds arrive at game start, and moving items in combat is free. Best for story and exploration.


• Normal — AMP as the author intended, and the recommended mode for most players. Enemies scale to your party's tier and bosses grow tougher, with boss-kill progression making the world a little meaner over time. The optional escalation systems (the Pyre, Battle Instinct and the combat item-move cost) start off, but can be flipped on from the Training Ring whenever you want more bite. A pity system catches bad salvage luck.


• Hard — for ultra-hardcore min-maxers who need to scratch that itch. Unfair conditions stacked against you, and that's the price of admission for the best gameplay. Enemies and bosses get serious bonuses — AoE evasion, chasm immunity, crit resistance, attack advantage and more — every escalation system is switched on and locked, the toughest bosses cheat death, and the economy tilts to compensate (more charges per capsule, but the reroll window slams shut fast, and the safety nets come off). In the late game a head-on fight with a group is practically a death sentence; you'll master split-pulling, stealth, and crowd control. Built for cheat runs and solo-duo Honour mode with deep mechanical understanding.

The Tier System

Every enemy's power tracks your party's average level, not its own. AMP blends the creature's level with your party's average — your party's level weighs heaviest — to read an effective level, then sorts it into one of six tiers: from Tutorial at the bottom, through Early Game, Midgame, Lategame and Endgame, up to Divine, the top tier reserved for level-20 content and custom god-bosses. Because it's your level driving the math, fights stay sharp from level 1 onward, and walking back into an old area won't trivialize it as harshly as you'd expect. Only playable companions who can level up count toward the average; summons, hirelings and temporary allies don't. Friendly and neutral creatures are tiered one step gentler, so your allies-of-convenience never outshine you.

What Each Mode Changes

The mode you pick quietly rewrites the rules behind the scenes: how many charges a capsule carries and how long its reroll window stays open, whether merchants refresh their artifacts, how many Interplanar Chests exist and whether they come pre-unlocked, the prices and stock of the Trials of Tav Shop, your salvage odds, the bad-luck pity system, the cost of moving items in combat, and whether bosses hand you bonus coins. Casual is generous on every axis; Hard is stingy on most but throws you extra capsule charges to survive its brutality.

Hard-Mode Comebacks

On Hard, and partly on Normal, several systems exist for one reason: to stop a fight from being solved by a single alpha-strike.


• Last Stand. The toughest foes get a one-time burst of temporary hit points when near death, so one big hit won't always finish them. Expect them to swing back.
• Death Defying. On Hard, the strongest bosses cheat death once: dropped to zero, they return stronger, with an extra action, life-drain and regeneration. Finish the job, then brace for round two.
• Eclipse. Some Hard bosses heal to full once at half health, with a burst of radiant light. Once per fight, but enough to undo a careless overextension.
• Battle Instinct. Bosses shrug off your opening burst. At the start of combat they gain Resistance to All Damage for one turn, so an alpha-strike can't end the fight before it begins. Optional on Normal, locked on Hard.

Calibration

Balance is built around duo/solo Honour mode — the most demanding format. A duo min-maxer in AMP has roughly 75% of the total firepower of a casual four-player party: AMP items deal far more damage per character, but two characters instead of four cuts total actions in half. For a full party it's significantly easier, which is why groups of 4 are recommended to switch to Hard mode by the end of Act 2.




6. Enemy Scaling and Progression


In Normal and Hard modes, a two-layer system ramps up the challenge as you advance.


• Base tier bonuses. Every creature receives fixed bonuses for its tier — accuracy, defense, health, and mobility, with the higher tiers adding extra actions, bonus damage, crit resistance, and immunity to being knocked prone or shoved into chasms. Bosses always sit a step above regular enemies. On Hard the bonuses are far heavier, layering on AoE evasion, fall-damage immunity, minimum-damage floors, attack advantage and more. The top Divine tier is a different animal entirely, built for level-20 mods and AMP's own god-bosses, and you'll know one when you see it.


• Progression from boss kills. Every time you kill one of the tracked story bosses, all enemies in the world — even ones you haven't met yet — gain a small permanent stack. Regular foes mostly gain health and speed; bosses gain more across the board. The catch is that each stack locks at the tier where it was earned: kill Ethel while you're low-level and that stack stays small forever, it never upgrades as you level up. After a dozen boss kills, every enemy carries a dozen overlapping stacks. Only a specific set of major bosses counts — elite enemies that merely feel boss-like don't trigger it. Casual disables progression entirely.


• The deliberate exclusions. Progression purposely leaves out the stats that break the game at high stack counts. Accuracy, critical hit threshold, and extra crit dice all live in the fixed base layer and never scale infinitely. This ensures that even after twenty boss kills the game stays tough but beatable, rather than turning into an automatic player wipe with zero counterplay.




7. The Pyre


The Pyre is a funeral rite that kindles only in boss battles. The fallen feed an otherworldly flame, and the harder and faster you press the fight, the higher it climbs through ten escalating stages. Its strength is hidden. You read the current stage as a status on your foes, so blitz a boss and the last things standing rise to meet you.

When it burns. Boss battles only; a boss must be in the fight. It is off on Casual, optional on Normal (flip it on from the Settings Ring), and always lit on Hard, where it climbs faster. It lingers a while in real time and survives stealth or flight, returning when the same foes re-enter combat. At low party levels the flame builds slowly and reaches full speed in the lategame.

How it rises. Wounding foes feeds it a little, kills feed it more, and a boss's death feeds it hugely. Hard crowd control and "cheese" statuses nudge it up too. Speed is the real fuel: overkill, multi-hits and fast kills stoke it hardest, while a measured pace lets it cool.

How it cools. Left alone it loses half its heat every round, so easing off the throttle lets it die down between turns. Acid and Radiant damage are your fire hose, and the first such hit each fight knocks it down a whole stage. Healing a marked foe, or breaking one with a failed Constitution Saving Throw, cools it further.

The ten stages. From a faint Spark the rite climbs through Smoulder, Embers, Flame, Blaze, Balefire, Conflagration, Wildfire and Gehenna, all the way to Inferno. Each stage hands every living enemy more accuracy, armour, damage and toughness; the higher ones grant extra actions, advantage, reactions and damage-soak, and at the very top near-immunity to control. At Inferno, even a common bandit fights at your level: it shrugs off your crowd control, strikes with advantage and several actions, and will not go down easily.

The lesson. Don't blitz what you can't finish. If a boss fight won't close quickly and cleanly, pace yourself and let the fire die between rounds, or keep Acid and Radiant on hand to put it out.




8. ULTRA Mode


ULTRA is a secret, opt-in overlay that stacks on top of whatever base mode you chose. It's for players who have mastered AMP and want the enemies to fight dirty.

Unlocking it. The game offers ULTRA the first time you kill an enemy after your host reaches level 8. Decline, and it is offered once more at level 12, then never again on its own. You can also unlock it early, at any level, from the Training Ring settings (Normal and Hard only). Accepting triggers a short fanfare, an electric-guitar sting, and there is no going back: once accepted, ULTRA stays on for the entire run.

What it does. Every enemy, present and future, gains an extra layer of stats on top of its tier: more armour, more health, more speed, sharper saving throws and extra damage on every strike. The layer is flat. Unlike boss-kill progression it never grows over the campaign, so it is a fixed surcharge on every fight rather than a snowball. Top-tier Apex foes that take no damage on their turn surge into an extra action on the next. On Casual the difficulty system doesn't track enemies, so ULTRA has nothing to attach to and changes nothing; it only bites on Normal and Hard. The party itself takes no penalty in the current build.

Mirror Support

ULTRA's signature. Once per fight, bring a weakened boss to its knees with hard crowd control, and a Mirror champion answers from the Void to fight at its side. One is summoned, drawn at random, each a genuine threat with its own trick and a clear counter. Slay the pursuer to claim its rare drops. They don't give up easily, and if you flee they will follow, so finish what you started.




9. Training Ring and Settings


The moment a new game begins, the Training Ring lands directly in your inventory, no hunting required. It looks like a gray-rarity nut with a bunch of built-in spells, and it's packed with extremely useful debugging functions for any player. Let's go through them:


• Summon the Chadd: one of the most important functions, letting you summon a real dummy for practicing combat and testing new experimental builds. It works almost like a real fight — except the enemy doesn't move and can barely hurt you (barely). You immediately receive all spell slots and tons of resources so you can test complex one-turn combos. One side effect: after the test ends you'll restore all spell slots you had before testing, keep that in mind. The dummy is removed the moment you "attack" another creature — anti-exploit protection for real combat.
• Summon Archer: unlike Chadd the dummy, this enemy can and will fight back. This time you won't get buffed and will have to use your own resources. Use it when you want to practice a real combat scenario against a ranged fighter with serious tools.
• Summon Berbalang: open a portal to the Astral Plane and summon a dangerous creature that'll put up a real fight. As a reward you can receive an Astral Coin, so in a way this is actual gameplay, not just testing.
• Kill the Chadd: instantly kill Chadd or the archer, ending combat.
• Summon Test Chests: extremely useful function to summon all magical items from vanilla + AMP. You can use this to browse missing pieces for your build, grab items after bugs/errors, or just straight-up cheat. Warning: summoning 2500 items at once can crash the game on weaker hardware!

The Setup Wizard

The first time you start a run, AMP walks you through a quick setup wizard, a short chain of prompts that lets you pick your game mode and switch the optional systems on or off before you dive in: tooltips, the merchant fix, the Trials of Tav Shop, the Pyre, auto-loot and auto-sell, the combat item-move cost, Battle Instinct and Avarice. Don't agonize over any of it. Everything the wizard asks can be changed later from the Settings Ring.

AMP Settings

All mode settings live in the Training Ring under AMP Settings, organized into categories:


• Tooltip Settings — choose from one of six popup modes you'll see when interacting with AMP systems. The second mode is set by default. If you're an experienced player who knows AMP well, go with the fourth. Whenever you pick a mode, all tooltips are completely reset and shown fresh.
• Game Mode — switch your game mode, described in detail in the "Game Modes" chapter.
• Trade Settings — toggle the merchant fix. This matters if you use mods that need their items showing up at merchants. Disabling the fix removes all AMP magic pools from merchants — so consider ParaTool, covered in the "Compatibility" chapter, to integrate other mods into AMP's loot pools instead.
• Trials of Tav Shop — enable or disable the special shop described in its own chapter.
• The Pyre — switch the boss-fight escalation fire on or off (Normal only; it's forced on for Hard and off for Casual). See the "Pyre" chapter.
• Avarice — the generosity toggle from the "Quest and Boss Rewards" chapter; off by default.
• Difficulty extras — flip Battle Instinct (a boss buff) and the combat item-move cost on or off, where your mode allows.
• ULTRA — unlock the secret overlay early instead of waiting for the level offer (Normal and Hard only). See the "ULTRA Mode" chapter.

Auto-Loot and Auto-Sell

Two quiet quality-of-life systems save you from clicking on every barrel. Auto-loot sweeps up junk (common weapons and armour, crockery, consumables and gold) from the ground, unlocked containers and corpses around you, but only while you're out of combat. It deliberately leaves real artifacts alone (anything valuable enough to matter), so it never grabs the gear you actually want; pick those up yourself. Auto-sell pairs with it: mark what you don't need and it's sold off at merchants automatically. Both are filter-driven and entirely optional, so set them up in the wizard or fine-tune them from the ring.




10. Technical Information


Here are the technical details of the mode that will help you better understand what's happening under the hood and avoid misunderstandings.


• REL Architecture (Randomized Equipment Loot). The system intercepts calls to vanilla loot tables and replaces them with its own, containing random items appropriate to the current level.
• Duplicates. Many items exist in 4 versions of different rarities, appearing at corresponding game stages. This lets you find a weak version of an interesting item in Act 1, and an upgraded legendary version of an early artifact later. The system increases variety without creating thousands of new items at low cost, multiplying replayability and possible combinations by millions.
• Merchants and the "_None" Loot List. After the first visit to a merchant followed by a long rest, their loot table is replaced with a "_None" version containing only consumables. This prevents infinite respawning of unique artifacts from the random pool. Check merchants carefully on first visit — their unique inventory won't refresh. This also affects third-party mods that add items to merchants — after a long rest, all their items will vanish if they didn't account for compatibility! In Casual mode, merchants always refresh their stock.
• No Dynamic Stat Generation. The engine doesn't allow creating items on-the-fly with random properties. All 2500+ items are handcrafted and exist as individual entities. That's exactly why I can't just "add more variations" — each item is hours of manual work. There is, however, an option for enchantments on top, as implemented in a new mod by my colleague UnWeave, which also supports AMP compatibility. On top of that, the Runic Shards system lets you upgrade weapons and give them dynamic properties!
• Non-Unique Items. All artifacts in the game are made non-unique, which while allowing them to appear an unlimited number of times per playthrough, enables deep category variation. This also means items don't persist in merchant inventories between refreshes — buy what you like immediately.

Remember: many "bugs" are actually engine limitations or misunderstanding of hidden mechanics. Knowing these details will help you enjoy the mode more and avoid unnecessary frustration from what seems like unfair randomness.




11. Trials of Tav Shop


The Trials of Tav Shop (a.k.a. Planar Emporium) is a special trading system originally built for the Trials of Tav mod by celerev, but also available in the regular campaign. You can enable or disable the shop through the Training Ring or when prompted at game start.

Once activated, Planar Emporiums — large magical barrels — appear in most camp locations. Open a barrel and it'll fill with a random assortment from three categories: Void Capsules, Planar Coins, and Runic Shards. All items are sold at triple the normal price. The shop offers a random number of items each time.

The shop refreshes after every long rest and also after you buy out its entire stock. You can sell items to the barrel too — just place an unwanted item inside and you'll receive a percentage of its value in gold. The buyback percentage depends on your game mode: Casual pays more, Hard pays significantly less. Stock size also varies by mode.

Keep in mind: using the Planar Emporium in the regular campaign gives you a definite advantage since it essentially lets you convert gold into AMP resources. If you want to preserve balance — use it wisely, or save it for Trials of Tav.




12. Interplanar Chests


As you explore the world, you'll stumble upon special chests with extremely high lockpicking difficulty. They look like ghostly chests glowing with astral light. They're elusive and appear in the most unexpected places, showing up no more than a few times per location.

What's inside these chests? The reward is big and tempting: special Void Capsules that let you pull specific random equipment from targeted categories. Search carefully — they're often hidden in hard-to-reach spots!

Chest quantity and accessibility depend on your game mode. In Casual mode there are significantly more chests and they're already unlocked — just find them. In Normal — standard quantity, and you'll need lockpicks or a special tool. In Hard — noticeably fewer chests.

There are three ways to open Interplanar Chests. First — traditional lockpicking with thieves' tools. Second — brute force destruction, though that's pretty tough to pull off (but possible). Third — hitting the chest with a special "lockpick." This lockpick can be found in the world. It's carefully hidden and doesn't look like a lockpick at all. A couple hints:

• It's purple (Very Rare) quality
• It's located away from sunlight
• It's in Act 1
• It can only be found with a Perception check




13. Compatibility


Think of mods in this game like layers of paint on a wall. Fun fact: even Honour mode is technically a mod. Picture a white wall — that's vanilla. Paint some sections red — that's Honour mode. Install AMP — now you've painted over some areas in purple. Add FED on top — certain spots turn green, covering parts of the purple. You only see the final layer of paint, and that's exactly how modding works in BG3.

This isn't about "compatibility" in the traditional sense — you won't get crashes or error messages. What happens is simpler: the paint underneath just won't be visible. There are some shared files that can't be edited dynamically at a granular level, so whichever mod loads last will always win by replacing those files with its own content.

But unlike a painter, you can control which layer of paint shows up on top. That's what load order is for, though you can't change it in the game's mod manager where everything runs alphabetically (which puts Ancient Mega Pack at a disadvantage). You'll need BG3MM — a dedicated mod manager — to control load order properly. I recommend always placing AMP lower in your load order than other mods so they don't accidentally paint over it.

When you install AMP, you're essentially replacing everything related to equipment and magical item distribution. Here's how different types of mods interact when they load after it:

Major equipment overhauls like FED: These mods do basically the same thing, so they'll completely break randomization in many areas, essentially defeating the whole purpose of using AMP. Plus they dump their own items on top, further breaking progression balance — the carefully tuned pace at which you acquire new gear. FED is particularly notorious for throwing legendary artifacts at you right at the start. Fortunately, there aren't many mods like this, and FED is pretty much the only one you need to worry about. I strongly recommend choosing either one or the other — not both.

Complete game overhauls like PHB2024: From what's been reported, these don't affect AMP too severely since they mostly work in different areas, only occasionally touching items at a non-invasive level. They might add new items to merchants or rebalance certain vanilla equipment. However, due to the merchant fix, these items will vanish after you long rest following a merchant visit (unless they're unique artifacts). PHB2024, for instance, is known for adding vanilla legendaries to Act 2 merchants, which breaks AMP's progression balance. Keep this in mind — it's best to place AMP lower in load order than PHB.

Major bugfix compilations: These mods act as comprehensive patches for everything Larian missed. They change a lot: from dialogue and quest lines to broken artifacts and their descriptions. The artifact fixes specifically are what you don't need with AMP. Over the years, I've done extensive work on vanilla equipment based on player feedback, fixing most known bugs and issues. Some artifacts were completely reworked from incredibly boring to incredibly fun and synergistic. Item descriptions also got positive updates. So these bugfixes should preferably load above AMP to prevent their scattered adjustments from conflicting with AMP's design philosophy.

Cosmetic mods: Don't affect AMP at all — actually, it's the opposite. If their creators add items to merchants (which AMP affects 100% by completely replacing loot lists), those additions will get wiped. Remember, you can always disable the merchant fix at campaign start if you want maximum compatibility.

Small equipment mods: Things like Elven Weaponry or Small Collection of My Homebrew Stuff, where authors add 1-20 new artifacts scattered around the world. Even small additions affect progression balance, so I don't recommend using them. Instead, I'd suggest reaching out to those authors about collaborating to integrate their collections into AMP's loot pools. But if you really want them in your game, you usually don't need to do anything — 99% of the time they'll load after AMP alphabetically and override its properties where they conflict.

ParaTool: you can now integrate all small and not-so-small equipment mods directly into AMP's loot pools! Just head to the AMP Discord server, follow the Github link, and install the app for Win 64/32 or Linux! ParaTool is dead simple and requires zero brain power to use.




14. History


My development journey began in August 2023. After playing several hours of BG3, I realized the itemization desperately needed improvement. I was especially shocked by the lack of cloaks, rings, and amulets. I'm not a Diablo fan (never actually played it), but come on — one and a half artifacts per Act? That's just laughable. Years later, I've come to understand that Larian simply never intended for this RPG to be about rich equipment choices. Just look at how they cut dozens of artifacts after release, not to mention the overall scarcity of synergies and possible combinations. Don't get me wrong — vanilla enthusiasts have been discovering new builds for years with their limited item pool, and there's still decent variety. But combine that with fixed item locations that unlock at specific stages, and the picture gets pretty stale for a roguelike fan where replayability hinges on how unpredictable your loot acquisition is.

So I immediately got to work on rings, using the old Arcane Rings mod as a foundation. While promising, it never grew beyond 40 items, all cheaply available from Arron right at the start. Not nearly enough. Back then it was either Arcane Rings or collections of legendary artifacts with game-breaking stats. I decided to take on the challenge of creating something relatively balanced, expanding early game variety, and obtained through immersive gameplay rather than Tutorial Chests or starter merchants.

My first experiments focused on rings and amulets (Ancient Jewelry), which naturally evolved into new weapons (Ancient Weaponry), armour (Ancient Armoury), and cloaks (Master's Cloaks — a fun addition featuring Lorroakan enchanting Baldurian cloaks in his basement during his spare time). These all relied on early randomization systems built directly into the collections (some veterans might still remember them on Nexus). Eventually I hit a major problem: all my collections distributed items separately, on top of vanilla items players were already getting. This created massive progression imbalances that needed urgent fixing. That's when I embarked on my most ambitious project — Randomized Equipment Loot.

I spent months building this mod, meticulously going through every game character, every chest, every corner — without the Toolkit, which modders could only dream of back then. The early version was rough, but it worked. It gave me the ability to integrate all my items alongside vanilla ones into a unified system with unified pools that the game would draw from whenever players opened chests or defeated bosses. Not everything could be randomized right away — I discovered many solutions much later, like quest reward randomization and character equipment. These required various workarounds that sometimes still cause minor issues, though nothing major. Some randomization limitations still exist in scripted rewards where I can't really control artifact distribution, so I nerfed them to avoid guaranteed power spikes.

This actually became my first major controversy. Toxic players started attacking my work, trying to convince others to avoid my mods. The issue was that before, players just needed to download equipment mods, but now they also needed REL, which affected vanilla drops. Despite the hate, popularity kept growing, and I pushed forward. Enthusiastic player reviews only strengthened my conviction that bringing roguelike elements to BG3 wasn't such a crazy idea. But considering the vocal minority of vanilla purists (there are still surprisingly many — honestly, I can't understand replaying something that gives you the exact same variables after 3000 hours), I simultaneously developed REL Light, keeping some lore equipment in place, and REL Ancient, providing all my items independently from vanilla.

Time went on, I added new content, continuously improved REL with significant adjustments. But maintaining three versions became a crushing burden — implementing the same functions across three different mods was exhausting. Eventually I did the math and decided to focus on one version. That version was my favorite and the one I believed in from the start — REL Full. It realized the dream of infinite chaos and discovery, complete randomization with carefully balanced RNG. The Light version was a compromise, not truly roguelike — some items stayed in place "just because," and many of them locked you into specific builds and metas. As for Ancient, progression balance went out the window since I couldn't predict item distribution and had to work around vanilla spawn points — plus it would've meant hundreds of wasted hours of REL development.

REL Full found its supporters and critics. Haters came out again, hurling abuse at my design choices — but popularity continued to grow. My philosophy was simple: if you love vanilla with its endlessly predictable loot, then play vanilla. Why come after me? I expanded several more collections and by summer 2024, I'd mostly stepped back from development, considering my work complete.

Everything changed when Larian released official modding tools in September 2024. We were all pretty skeptical — I remember discussing it with GraphicFade, and we both agreed that if there wasn't a smooth conversion path to the toolkit and mod.io, we wouldn't do the work twice. But we also agreed that a platform with one-click mod installs from within the game would kill Nexusmods for BG3. And it nearly did, except for Script Extender mods that weren't allowed on mod.io.

I wasn't planning to do anything beyond a few critical updates. Then suddenly, someone posted REL and all Ancient collections on mod.io. I was stunned — did someone manually recreate all those items from scratch in that terrible interface? Turns out it was simple. Conversion was easy — users figured it out themselves since Larian hadn't told any modders about it. But instead of migrating all these countless mods one by one, I decided to go all-in — Ancient Mega Pack.

I spent a long time choosing the name. It needed to show direct lineage from my previous work (hence Ancient), while conveying the collection's scope and superiority over everything else combined (Mega Pack). Ancient Mega Pack was born. It also had simple international appeal — practically everyone knows Mega, Pack, and Ancient.

I committed to a complete overhaul — not just the structure but individual elements too: every item icon was reworked, massive rebalancing was done, hundreds of new items were added, and the built-in REL architecture was significantly improved. You'd laugh if you saw what existed before AMP — the quality was amateur hour at best. Now this was a comprehensive All-in-One solution available with a single click. No worrying about load order, multiple versions, or agonizing choices. Download and play. Peak modding convenience, almost like official DLC. And honestly, that's how I see it now — the scale and quality are comparable to something the developers themselves might have made.

The new unified collection quickly gained traction (as Fade and I predicted) because entering such a broad market opened access to the "casual" audience — people who don't understand "all that Nexus stuff," don't know what a mod manager is, and don't want to think about it. Open the Mods tab, click a button, boom — random loot. The real turning point came in February 2025 when AMP was approved for consoles. Since then, this new game mode hasn't left the front pages of popular mods, and after Patch 8 dropped on April 15, it experienced another boom, climbing into the top 3 best mods of all time on mod.io, where it still regularly appears.

I genuinely hope this work will let players enjoy BG3 for decades and thousands of hours to come!

And one last thing. As you read this, active development has come to a close — AMP is complete, and there won't be new mechanics or collections beyond what you're holding. If three years of this solo work brought you joy, and you feel like saying thanks, you can toss me a single dollar on Boosty: boosty.to/paramonovgames. It's entirely optional and changes nothing in the mod — just a small way to support a project that ate years of my life. Either way, thank you for playing.

Q: Where did the adamantine moulds go?
A: Since they grant access to some of the strongest artifacts in the game, they've been randomized too. Fortunately, you can only find them in the Grymforge/Underdark area. On average you'll find 4 moulds, but there's no guarantee which ones. If you enable Casual mode, all moulds are teleported to you at game start.

Q: How do I get the Training Ring if I lost it?
A: Summon the Tutorial Chest! Yeah, it's that easy. There are tons of mods for this in the manager, just search: Tutorial Chest — and install any of them. You can also find the ring for sale from Volo and Rolan.

Q: The tooltips are driving me crazy, how do I turn them off?
A: Open AMP Settings in the Training Ring → Tooltip Settings and pick the mode that works for you.

Q: How do I change the game mode?
A: Open AMP Settings in the Training Ring → Game Mode.

Q: What's the Pyre? My enemies suddenly got terrifying in the middle of a boss fight.
A: It's a hidden fire that builds during boss battles the faster you blitz, empowering every surviving enemy through ten stages. Ease off the pace, or hit foes with Acid and Radiant to cool it down. Full details in the "Pyre" chapter.

Q: A mini-boss appeared in the middle of my fight and started chasing me. What is that?
A: That's ULTRA's Mirror Support, a secret overlay you opted into. A cornered boss called in a Mirror champion. Kill the summoned pursuer for bonus rewards. See the "ULTRA Mode" chapter.

Q: What is Avarice?
A: An optional generosity toggle that makes boss rewards richer and stocks merchants with bonus loot. Off by default; flip it from AMP Settings. See "Quest and Boss Rewards".

Q: Items are getting picked up and sold on their own. Is that a bug?
A: No — that's auto-loot and auto-sell, which you can configure or turn off in AMP Settings. They only grab junk and leave real artifacts for you.

Q: I can't click the Accept button on quest rewards, the hotbar is covering it?
A: Try minimizing the hotbar by clicking the Minus icon at the bottom right. If that doesn't help, make sure you're using a modern monitor, or install Vova's Hotbar.

Q: How do I download an older version?
A: Go to the mod's page on mod.io, find the file history on the right side, and download the version you need using the changelog as reference. This is useful if you're playing with a console friend and need matching versions.

Q: My game is crashing and I think it's because of AMP?
A: This can happen in combat with mods that increase the party size limit. It used to be an issue but shouldn't be anymore. If nothing helps, switch to Casual mode.

Q: PS5 update won't download?
A: Try tethering through your phone's mobile data — I've heard that gets the download to work.

Q: The console version is behind, when will you update it?
A: It's already updated. If the version is behind — that's entirely on Larian, since they're the ones who need to hit the Approve button.

Q: Where did ring and weapon crafting go?
A: Removed a long time ago.

Q: Where did the camp stations and the big altar go?
A: Removed a long time ago.

Q: What does "also" and "additionally" mean in effect descriptions?
A: "Also" means the damage is a damage rider, i.e. bonus damage, while "additionally" means the damage is standalone. Bonus damage needs something to attach to, and some damage sources may refuse riders entirely — while standalone damage can collect bonus damage on top of itself.

Q: How do we split loot between players?
A: I dunno, roll a die or something?

Q: Can I disable one specific feature?
A: Many of the optional systems can be switched off in AMP Settings. For anything not exposed there, you'd need to create a submod and remove it on your end.

Q: I installed AMP mid-playthrough, should I start over?
A: Yes.

Q: If I don't like it, can I remove everything?
A: Yes, but your save might break. You'll also obviously lose all items. The game typically crashes at 83% loading.

Q: How does difficulty progression work? Why did enemies get stronger?
A: Every fight scales to your party's average level, and on top of that, each major boss kill gives all enemies a small permanent stack. This works in Normal and Hard modes. Details in the "Enemy Scaling and Progression" chapter.

Q: Any recommendations for a 4-player co-op group?
A: Start with Normal mode. Toward the end of Act 2, you can switch to Hard through the Training Ring — four characters geared up with AMP artifacts will be plenty strong by then.

Q: What's a Planar Emporium / that shop thing in camp?
A: That's the Trials of Tav Shop — a big barrel where you can buy capsules, coins, and shards for gold. More details in its own chapter.

Q: If I update AMP on an existing save, will all the new features work?
A: Most of them — yes, but new scripted features (new quest rewards, new boss reward windows, new shard mechanics) require a fresh playthrough. This is a fundamental limitation of Osiris scripts, which don't carry over to existing saves.

A small sun-shaped pendant of celestial gold, its citrine center catching light even in shadow. A temple acolyte pawned it for bread money; the pawnbroker's nightmares stopped the day he sold it. The rays are sharp enough to draw blood.

Temple artificers of Lathander shaped this solar medallion from gold blessed at high noon, its citrine heart pulsing with trapped dawn. The sharp ray-spikes around the stone are not decorative — they channel divine light into darkness. Those who sleep wearing it dream only of sunrise.

The Dawnbringers forged this sacred sun when Lathander's light first pierced the Shadowfell's border. The celestial gold was smelted in prayers; the citrine was cut from a fallen star. Three saints wore it into darkness and returned. The fourth did not return — but neither did the darkness. The ray-spikes glow when undeath is near, burn when undeath is afraid.
The sun does not shine upon this talisman. The talisman shines upon the sun.

A pendant of fire-blackened steel, its cracked ruby leaking faint golden light through the fractures. Found in the crater where a Netherese tower once stood. The metal is warm, the stone surprisingly heavy. Graviturgists sense something vast sleeping within.

Netherese battlemages forged this pendant from steel exposed to pure destruction, setting a fractured ruby at its heart. Golden light seeps from the cracks — not escaping, but threatening. The charred surface bears symbols in a language that predates words. Scholars who study it too long develop headaches that bend inward.

Grumbar's faithful recovered this pendant from the void between planes, where destruction had worn through reality itself. The cracked ruby pulses with primordial force — the power that existed before creation learned restraint. The golden rays escaping the fractures are not light but pressure, weight made visible. The charred steel bears scratches from something that tried to contain what cannot be contained.
The pendant does not hang from its chain. The chain hangs from it.

A round silver medallion with a blue opal at its center, its wavy edges suggesting frozen sound. Inside the stone, something flickers — a tiny storm that never ends. Sailors pay fortunes for such things; the seas respect those who carry tempests.

Storm-priests of Talos shaped this eye-of-the-storm medallion from silver struck by divine lightning, setting a blue opal at its heart where an eternal tempest rages. The wavy edges channel sound into focused devastation. Hair rises near it on dry days. Those struck by lightning while wearing it feel only validation.

This medallion was torn from the sky during Talos's Fury — the storm that drowned Old Cormyr's fleet. The blue opal contains a hurricane's living eye, still spinning, still hungry. The High Stormherald wore it when he spoke with the god directly; he never shared what was said. The wavy silver edges amplify his whispers into thunder.
There is no thunder when this pendant strikes. Thunder comes after, apologizing for its tardiness.

An egg-shaped pendant cradled in obsidian scales, its fire opal heart flickering with something that might be movement. A dying pyromancer's last project — he swore he saw wings forming in the stone. The scales are warm, the opal warmer. Something wants to hatch.

Firewalker cultists shaped this nest-pendant from obsidian scales, setting a fire opal at its heart where a phoenix embryo slowly forms. They waited generations for the hatching. The phoenix never emerged — but the ember never cooled. It grants uncomfortable kinship with flames; they bend toward the wearer like flowers toward sun.

Nine master smiths forged this dragon-nest pendant in Kossuth's sacred forge, each adding a layer of obsidian scales before passing it on. The tenth smith was the Lord of Flames himself, who breathed life into the fire opal's heart. A phoenix dances within the stone now — born of living flame, never dying, never quite hatching. Fire becomes a companion, not a threat — and companions protect their own.
The pendant does not burn. Burning is what lesser flames do.

An uncut crystal of eternal ice set between two white dragon fangs, its bronze frame perpetually frosted. The topaz — if topaz it truly is — never warms. A Reghedman shaman traded it for safe passage; he seemed relieved to be rid of it. The fangs are real.

Auril's winter-priests set this crystal of absolute zero between fangs pulled from Arauthator himself, binding ice to ice in bronze that grows frost in any weather. The topaz glows with cold that existed before fire was invented. Those who wear it too long dream of glaciers — and the glaciers dream back.

The Frostmaiden's highest priestess wore this pendant when she walked naked into the Endless Winter and emerged three years later, unchanged. The dragon fangs framing the crystal are from Arveiaturace's first kill; the topaz contains temperature so low it borders on philosophy. She claimed Auril had kissed her. The kiss remains, crystallized in the stone. Cold becomes a cloak, not a threat — and the cloak is jealous.
The pendant is not cold. Cold is what exists when this pendant is absent.

An egg-shaped pendant of silver worked into dragon coils, its dark emerald pulsing with sickly green light. A graverobber found it clutched in a lich's hand; the lich was truly dead, but the pendant was not. The silver is cold as tomb-stone.

Netherese death-speakers bound a fragment of the Negative Energy Plane within this emerald of undeath, caging it in silver dragon coils that contain what should not be contained. The stone glows with swamp-fire — the light of things rotting in dark places. Those who die nearby linger a moment longer than they should.

Myrkul himself blessed this cage-pendant when he took dominion over the dead, marking it as passage-right through his realm. The silver coils are cold with purpose; the emerald burns with unlife. Three Lord Knights of the Eternal Order wore it while escorting souls to judgment. The dead recognize its bearer as kindred — or master. The line blurs.
Death is not the opposite of life. This pendant is the opposite of both.

A shield-shaped pendant of battle-scarred steel, its amber heart flickering with trapped flame. Found after the Battle of Bones, still warm, still angry. The obsidian frame bears scratches from weapons that no longer exist. The black iron chain weighs like responsibility.

Tempus's war-priests hammered this shield-pendant from blued steel collected after the Horde Wars, setting an amber stone where ancient battle-flame still burns. The spiked corners have drawn blood from careless handlers. Those who wear it find their reflexes quickening before danger arrives — the amber remembers when to fight.

The First General of Tempus wore this war-pendant at the Battle of the Gods, when mortals dared to challenge divinity. He did not win. But neither did the gods. The amber contains flame from that battle — still burning, still defiant. The massive black iron chain is forged from weapons of fallen heroes. The pendant echoes with a thousand battles, and each echo teaches something useful.
The pendant does not grant victory. Victory was always the bearer's. The pendant merely reminds them.

A peridot crystal the color of concentrated acid, set in brass bands that show signs of slow corrosion. An apprentice alchemist's final project before her disappearance. The Celtic knot-work on the frame is being gradually simplified by fumes only the stone can smell.

Netherese transmuters crystallized this peridot from pure aqua regia, binding entropy in brass bands that will eventually lose their war against the stone. The yellow-green crystal sweats vapor that etches glass. Alchemists who study it develop an uncomfortable appreciation for impermanence.

Ghaunadaur's blind prophets grew this pendant in vats of universal solvent, letting the peridot form from concentrated dissolution. The brass bands are the third set — the first two surrendered to the stone's patient hunger. It dissolves the boundary between what was and what will be. Decay becomes a tool, not a fate.
The pendant does not corrode. Existence corrodes away from it.

A medallion of soot-darkened steel with concentric ridges, its star sapphire heart flickering with violet light. It vibrates at frequencies felt in teeth and bones. Musicians find it fascinating; soldiers find it unsettling. The silver cord hums.

Akadi's wind-singers forged this medallion from steel exposed to thunderclaps, its concentric ridges designed to focus and amplify sound. The star sapphire contains violet lightning — not electrical, but gravitational, sound made visible. The architectural projections on its frame are antennae, tuning reality's vibrations. Those who wear it hear whispers in the wind — not voices, but something trying to become voices.

This heart-medallion was forged when thunder and lightning separated at the dawn of storms, each going their own way. Thunder got the worse bargain — power without flash — but learned to resent it. The star sapphire contains that resentment, violet and hungry. The bearer speaks with the voice of hurricanes. Silence becomes a choice, not a default.
The pendant makes no sound. Sound comes from the pendant.

A hexagonal pendant of tarnished copper, its amethyst heart pulsing with violet rhythm. The bone inlays around the stone form patterns that suggest brain matter. A mind-mage's apprentice piece — she said it whispered to her. She wasn't wrong.

Mind-mages of fallen Jhaamdath sealed a sleeping consciousness within this hexagonal pendant, the bone reliefs around the amethyst mimicking the folds of an Elder Brain. The consciousness forgot its wisdom but remembered how to want. It presses against the wearer's thoughts, curious and hungry. The copper has developed veins.

The Drowsing Emperor wore this seal-pendant when he ruled a kingdom that existed only in shared dreams. His subjects slept for centuries, living lives of impossible beauty in their minds. When he finally woke, he found his kingdom starved to death around him. The amethyst remembers what perfect dreams cost — and offers them anyway. The bone inlays are from Elder Brains who died dreaming.
The pendant does not think. Thinking happens to the pendant, and some of it leaks out.

An ampule-pendant of age-greened brass, its ruby heart seeming to flow inside the glass. The organic tendrils on the frame suggest veins or roots. Surgeons find themselves reaching for it without knowing why. The crystal pulses like a heartbeat.

Bhaal's cultists sealed a murderer's last heartbeat within this reliquary-pendant, watching it crystallize into ruby that still flows as if alive. The brass has aged green with centuries; the spikes around the frame have tasted blood. It grants uncomfortable awareness of nearby vitality — every heartbeat in the room becomes audible.

The Lifewell priests sealed a spring of vital essence within this ampule, drawing from the positive energy plane itself. The ruby is Bhaal's own blood, crystallized but still flowing, still hungry. It was meant to heal; it heals too well. Wounds close whether the bearer wills it or not. Life persists past its welcome. The sacrificial knife motifs on the brass are not symbolic.
The pendant does not contain blood. Blood contains a portion of the pendant, in everyone, everywhere.

Earrings of blackened steel, their teardrop obsidians catching light that isn't there. The night-stone beads on the chains click with sounds that seem to come from elsewhere. Thieves pay well for such trinkets, claiming they help with stealth. They don't — but believing they do often has the same effect.

Shar's faithful captured fragments of the Shadowfell's essence within these obsidian teardrops, binding darkness that had never known light. The filigree frames are worked into patterns that hurt to follow. The shadows they cast are darker than geometry explains. Things hidden in those shadows stay hidden longer than they should.

These whisper-earrings were worn by the Nightsinger — Shar's most devoted voice, who spoke only in darkness and sang only at midnight. They say she vanished into her own shadow one night and never returned. The obsidians hold violet hints of the Shadowfell; the night-stone beads whisper her songs to those who listen.
The earrings do not create shadow. Shadow is what exists when the earrings permit light.

A teardrop pendant of tarnished silver, its dark emerald clouded with inclusions that seem to move. The woven snake-scale patterns on the frame feel wrong under fingers. Herbalists recognize it; survivors respect it. The metal smells faintly of almonds.

Talona's plague-priests set this Colombian emerald with its poison inclusions in silver worked to mimic serpent scales. The dark clouds within the stone shift slowly, seeking. The snake-skin patterns on the frame are not carved — they grew there. Those who wear it rarely sicken; the charm prefers to give rather than receive.

The Merciful Suffering — Talona's highest blessing — rests within this serpent-pendant. It was worn by the plague doctor who ended the Weeping Death by spreading something worse. The emerald's inclusions are Talona's own venom, forever circulating. The pendant understands that some poisons heal, some medicines kill, and the only difference is dosage.
The pendant is not poison. Poison is how the pendant says hello.

A teardrop diamond set in platinum polished to impossible perfection. No fingerprints mar the surface; no light fails to find its way through. Wizards sense the Weave flowing more smoothly nearby. The stone is slightly warm — blood temperature, precisely.

Netherese theorists cut this diamond from pure magical essence, setting it in platinum that reflects light in ways that suggest other spectra. The stone refracts spells that pass near it, bending magic like light through water. Wizards find their incantations completing themselves in its presence.

Mystra herself blessed this teardrop diamond when she took dominion over the Weave, polishing the platinum with her own thought. Three Chosen wore it while reshaping reality. The Weave treats its bearer as a friend — or at least as someone worth impressing.
The pendant does not contain magic. Magic contains a fragment of the pendant, in every spell ever cast.

A band of celestial gold crowned with a pyramidal topaz that catches light from sources that shouldn't exist. Temple acolytes wear these; they rarely know why, only that shadows seem to avoid their hands.

The Luminarch — Lathander's supreme priest during the Time of Troubles — wore this sacred ring through the godswar. The pyramidal topaz has tasted divine light directly. The sacred reliefs on the golden band depict forces of good triumphant. It glows faintly at dawn, brighter at noon, and never truly dims.

When Elysium's gates opened during the Celestial Incursion, three stars fell to Faerun. This ring contains one, cut into a pyramid and set in celestial gold blessed by divine fire. It was blessed thrice — once by a solar, once by a deva, once by a mortal who had earned the right. Undeath withers in its presence. Death itself hesitates.
The ring does not shine. The sun shines because the ring permits it.

A band of electrum shattered into sharp angles, with a sphere of clear quartz at its heart. Inside the sphere, something flickers — tiny white bolts that never stop dancing. The cracks in the metal glow faintly blue.

The Voltaic Tyrant — a storm giant king who nearly conquered the Sword Coast — wore this shattered ring as proof of his authority over lightning. When he fell, the ring did not. The quartz sphere contains a storm that has raged for centuries. It still expects obedience.

Thunder's Dominion passed through the hands of seven Storm Lords before it found a mortal worthy of wearing it. Each lord added a blessing; each blessing added a bolt to the quartz sphere's eternal storm. The ring speaks in seven simultaneous whispers when lightning is near. The electrum shards cut those who grasp it without permission.
The ring does not call lightning. Lightning calls the ring for permission.

A band of obsidian steel that glows faintly red from within, scattered with garnets that catch light like embers. The spiral patterns suggest frozen flame. The metal is warm — pleasantly so, unless you're unwelcome.

The Primordial Inferno trapped within this ring was captured during the last eruption of Mount Hotenow — not the lava, but the fury that drove it. The garnets blazing around its circumference are arranged in spiral flame patterns. The ring does not burn its wearer. It burns everything else if asked.

Phoenix-priests of Kossuth pass this rebirth-ring from generation to generation, each wearing it until their death — then their successor pulls it from their ashes, garnets still blazing. It has been reborn fourteen times. The obsidian steel remembers each death and found them all instructive.
The ring does not burn. Burning is what happens when the ring remembers what fire used to mean.
A band of frosted mithril set with a crystal that might be ice, might be diamond — the cold makes it hard to tell. Frozen spikes ring the stone like a crown. The metal never warms, even against skin.

This signet bears the frost-pattern of Reality's Edge — the moment when existence meets absolute zero and stops pretending. It was carved from ice that had never known warmth. The frozen water spikes around the diamond are tears from a white dragon, crystallized mid-fall. The ring makes nearby water hesitate before boiling.

The Arctic Veil separates life from the cold that would claim it. Three Frostmaidens wore this ring before passing it to the mortal who earned their respect — by surviving a winter that killed gods. The diamond of absolute cold is surrounded by spikes of frozen time. The ring crystallizes threats around the bearer, buying precious moments.
The ring is not cold. Absolute zero is what happens when the ring gets bored.

A band of tarnished silver veined with something the color of rot, its emerald pulsing with sickly green light. The death-signs on the shank are in no living language. The metal is cold as gravestone.

The Soul Harvester's guild passed this signet between members, each adding a necrotic vein before their death. Seventeen souls contributed before the guild fell. The emerald glows with undead light; the silver is cold with stolen life. The ring whispers in seventeen voices when death is near.

Myrkul's heralds wear this death-ring as proof of their divine mandate — the authority to speak for the Judge of the Dead. The emerald radiates unlife; the necrotic veins pulse with the rhythm of stopped hearts. Three heralds have pronounced judgment while wearing it. All three judgments stuck, even against gods.
The ring does not command death. Death asks the ring for instructions.

A band of volcanic obsidian worked smooth by hellfire, its fire opal heart blazing with inner heat. The runes on its surface glow faintly — not Elvish, something older and angrier. The metal is warm, and dreams of battle follow it.

The Supreme General of the last Crusade wore this obsidian signet until her final battle — a fight she won despite dying. The fire runes in Black Speech glow brighter when blood is spilled nearby. The ring passed to her successor, then the next, then the next. It has commanded seventeen campaigns without a defeat.

Tempus himself blessed this war-ring during the Time of Troubles, pressing his thumb into the volcanic glass. The thumbprint remains, glowing with the fire opal's heat. The Black Speech runes are warnings to any who would face the bearer. Wars fought while wearing it tend to end quickly, decisively, and in the wearer's favor.
The ring does not grant victory. It reminds the wearer that defeat was never really an option.
A band of yellow-green amber, translucent as concentrated acid. The surface is uneven, seemingly corroded by its own nature. Inside the resin, ancient alchemical symbols float, frozen mid-equation.

The Molecular Decay that ended the Netherese floating city of Sanctuary is trapped within this amber signet — not acid itself, but the principle that allowed stone to forget it was solid. The alchemical script inside still writhes slowly, still calculating. The ring makes nearby metals uneasy.

Ghaunadaur's deepest priests pass this decay-ring between themselves, each wearing it until their body becomes too fluid to maintain the shape. The amber grows more translucent with each bearer; the alchemical script inside becomes more complex. The ring understands that all forms are temporary, and offers to hasten the inevitable.
The ring does not dissolve. Existence dissolves when the ring loses interest.

A band of dark crystal the color of storm-clouds, studded with obsidian spikes that seem to vibrate. The aggressive design suggests a weapon more than jewelry. The metal hums at frequencies felt in bones.

The Harmonic Chaos that shattered the Crystal Tower of Evereska is bound within this spiked ring — not the sound, but the principle that allowed vibration to become destruction. The obsidian resonators focus and amplify. The ring makes nearby glass uncomfortable.

This resonance-ring was forged at the exact moment thunder first separated from lightning — the instant when sound decided it needed no flash to matter. Seven storm lords blessed its obsidian spikes. The ring speaks with all their voices when reality needs to listen.
The ring makes no sound. Sound is what happens when the ring has something to say.

A band of tarnished copper wrapped around an amethyst that pulses with violet rhythm. The bone inlays form shapes that suggest brain matter — a gift, supposedly, from something that thought too much. The metal vibrates slightly against thoughts.

The Illithid Cerebral Matrix contained within this ring was extracted from an Elder Brain that died dreaming of freedom. The bone reliefs are fragments of that brain, still processing. The dreams persist. The ring whispers suggestions that are usually helpful and occasionally terrifying.

This mind-ring links the wearer to the Infinite Consciousness — the theoretical network of all thinking beings. The amethyst pulses with psionic waves; the bone brain-patterns around it serve as antenna. The connection is faint, like hearing a crowd from a great distance. But the crowd hears back.
The ring does not think. All thinking occurs within the ring, and some of it leaks out.

A massive band of blackened brass, its huge ruby the color of dried blood. The claws that hold the stone seem to grip rather than set it. Bhaal's symbols are worked into the metal. The ruby pulses when held.

The Bloodlord's Authority was passed between the high priests of Bhaal until the god's first death. Each priest's heartbeat is captured in the scattered rubies around the main stone. It remembers each heartbeat. The ring quickens when violence is near — not in warning, but in anticipation.

Seven murders consecrated this sovereign ring — not random killings, but precise sacrifices offered by those who understood what they were purchasing. Bhaal's symbols glow faintly when blood is spilled. The ring grants authority over life itself: where it goes, how fast it flows, when it ends.
The ring does not contain blood. All blood contains a fragment of the ring.

A band of darkened adamantine set with an obsidian that seems to contain depths. Violet hints swirl within — not reflections, something else. Thieves wear these believing they aid stealth; the belief helps more than the ring, but the ring helps too.

The Clinging Shadow bound within this gothic ring was captured from a demon's dying darkness — the last secret it tried to hide. The obsidian's violet swirls are hints of the Shadowfell bleeding through. The ring makes shadows deeper than geometry allows. Hidden things stay hidden longer.

Shar's Infiltrators pass this shadow-ring between agents, each adding a layer of darkness before passing it on. Seventeen layers now coat the obsidian's depths; the violet swirls are echoes of Shar herself. No one remembers what the original looked like. It's possible no one ever saw it clearly.
The ring casts no shadow. Shadows are what exist when the ring tolerates light.

A serpent of blackened mithril coiled around a clouded emerald, its peridot eye glowing faintly. The snake's scales are individually carved; its head seems poised to strike. The inclusions in the emerald move when observed closely.

This serpent-ring contains venom that has never found anything it couldn't corrupt — including previous owners. The emerald's poison inclusions swim slowly through the stone; the mithril snake's peridot eye tracks movement. Three alchemists died creating it, two from poison, one from irony. The ring respects commitment.

Talona's chosen wear this serpent-ring as proof of her blessing — the gift of understanding that poison and medicine are the same thing viewed from different angles. The snake's scales are individual prayers to corruption; its emerald heart contains venom from every poisonous creature. The ring ensures the wearer is always viewing from the correct angle.
The ring is not poisonous. Poison is how the ring shows affection.

An elegant band of polished platinum bearing a flawless brilliant in a six-claw setting. The metal reflects light perfectly — too perfectly, as if assisted. Mages sense the Weave flowing more smoothly near it.

The Stellar Radiance trapped within this signet was captured from a dying star — not its light, but its purpose. The flawless diamond catches light from spectra that shouldn't exist. The mirror-polished platinum reflects futures rather than faces. The ring makes magic easier, smoother, more willing to cooperate.

Mystra's Chosen wear this platinum ring as proof of her favor — the blessing of understanding that magic isn't a tool but a living thing that wants to be helpful. The six claws holding the diamond are not metal but crystallized will. The ring introduces the wearer to the Weave, personally.
The ring does not channel magic. Magic channels through everything because the ring suggested it might be fun.

Between the crystal spheres that contain worlds floats the phlogiston — a luminous, flammable chaos that ignites at the touch of open fire and burns until nothing remains. Spelljammer captains fear it. Arcane pyromancers covet it. This torch somehow contains a fragment, tamed but not tamed, burning with colors that shouldn't exist and heat that remembers the spaces between stars.
